The result depends on $a$, so different members have different axes.

$$a = 1$$

$$x$$

$$x=-1$$

$$a=2$$

$$a=-\frac{1}{2}$$

The axis slides as the Leitkoeffizient changes.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**E.** → Wahr

The crossing mit the vertical coordinate axis is the value at $x=0$, und the parameter multiplies $x^{2}$, which vanishes there.

$$g_{a}(0)=a\cdot 0+2\cdot 0-3$$

$$g_{a}(0)=-3$$

So every member of the family reaches the same height at $x=0$, however large or small the Leitkoeffizient is.

$$a = 1$$

$$g_{1}(0)$$

$$g_{a}(0)=-3$$

$$a=-5$$

$$h=g_{-5}(0)$$

$$h=-3$$

The whole family therefore pivots through the single point $(0,-3)$.

All of them cross the $y$-axis at that same point.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
MATH 7.85.solution_overview:
A one-parameter family of parabolas $g_a(x)=ax^{2}+2x-3$ mit $a\neq 0$ is compared mit the fixed line $f(x)=x+1$.

Rekonstruiere hier einmal die gemeinsame Gerade und Parabel; jeder Buchstabe prüft nur die in seiner Behauptung genannte Zusatzrechnung.

$g_a-f=ax^{2}+x-4$ mit discriminant $1+16a$; all curves pass through $(0,-3)$.

$$
ax^{2}+2x-3-(x+1) = ax^{2}+x-4 = 0
$$

$$\Delta(a)=1+16a$$

$$
1+16a = 0\implies a = -\frac{1}{16}
$$

MATH 7.86.title: Koeffizientenabgleich gegen eine Verknüpfung
MATH 7.86.context: Read the line $f(x)=5x+1$ und the parabola $g(x)=3x^{2}-2x-1$. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Das Anpassen von $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ erzwingt $A=\frac{3}{25}$.
Das Anpassen von $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ erzwingt $B=-2$.
Die höchste Potenz von $x$ in der verschachtelten Funktion $f(g(x))$ ist $x^{2}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Write $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ mit the given line $f(x)=5x+1$. Only the first summand can create an $x^{2}$ term, und squaring the line contributes $25x^{2}$.

$$A\cdot 5^{2}=3$$

$$A=\frac{3}{25}$$

The division is legitimate because the slope $5$ is non-zero, und no other value of $A$ can reproduce the Leitkoeffizient $3$ of $g$.

Matching forces $A=\frac{3}{25}$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Falsch

With $A=\frac{3}{25}$ already forced by the $x^{2}$ terms, equate the coefficients of $x$ in $A(5x+1)^{2}+B(5x+1)+C$ und in $g(x)=3x^{2}-2x-1$.

$$A(25x^{2}+10x+1)+B(5x+1)+C=3x^{2}-2x-1$$

The coefficient of $x$ on the left is $10A+5B$, und it must equal $-2$.

$$10\cdot\frac{3}{25}+5B = -2$$

$$x=\frac{6}{5}+5B$$

$$x=-2$$

$$B$$

$$A(25x^{2}+10x+1)+B(5x+1)+C=-\frac{16}{25}$$

The forced value is $-\frac{16}{25}$, not the claimed $-2$.

Matching does not force $B=-2$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**C.** → Wahr

Applying the line to the parabola multiplies the parabola by the slope und then addiert the intercept, so no new power of $x$ can sein created.

$$f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)=5(3x^{2}-2x-1)+1$$

Expanding the bracket keeps the highest power exactly where it was.

$$f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)=15x^{2}-10x-4$$

The highest power is $x^{2}$ mit coefficient $15\neq 0$.

The nested function is again a parabola.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**D.** → Wahr

A nested value is computed von the inside outwards: evaluate the inner function at the given number first, then feed the result into the outer function.

$$f(0)=5\cdot 0+1$$

$$f(0)=1$$

That output now becomes the input of $g$.

$$g(1)=3\cdot 1^{2}-2\cdot 1-1$$

$$1^{2}=1$$

$$g(1)=3\cdot 1-2\cdot 1-1$$

$$g(1)=0$$

Der verschachtelte Wert ist $0$.

$g(f(0))=0$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**E.** → Falsch

Nesting is not symmetric: feeding the line into the parabola need not agree mit feeding the parabola into the line, so each order has to sein computed on its own.

$$g(0)=-1$$

$$f(-1)=5\cdot(-1)+1$$

$$f(-1)=-4$$

$$f(0)=1$$

$$g(1)=3-2-1$$

$$g(1)=3-2$$

$$g(1)=1$$

$$g(1)=1-1$$

$$g(1)=0$$

The two orders give $-4$ und $0$, which are different numbers.

$f(g(0))\neq g(f(0))$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
MATH 7.86.solution_overview:
Both rules are handed over mit numbers already in place:

$$
f(x) = 5 x + 1,\qquad g(x) = 3 x^{2} - 2 x - 1
$$

Rewriting $g$ as $a(x-h)^{2}+k$ exposes the vertex, mit $h$ taken von the axis formula und $k$ obtained by substituting that abscissa back in.

$$
g(x) = 3\left(x-\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2}-\frac{4}{3},\qquad \text{vertex} = \left(\frac{1}{3},-\frac{4}{3}\right)
$$

Because $f$ is a line mit non-zero slope, the square $f(x)^{2}$ already carries an $x^{2}$ term, so $g$ can sein rebuilt von $f(x)^{2}$, $f(x)$ und a constant. Matching coefficients gives

$$
A = \frac{3}{25},\qquad B = -\frac{16}{25},\qquad C = -\frac{12}{25}
$$

MATH 7.87.title: Wurzelabstand gegen die Achse einer Parabel
MATH 7.87.context: The parabola $p$ is given by $p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Der Abstand zwischen den beiden Wurzeln von $p$ beträgt $13$.
Die Symmetrieachse von $p$ ist die Gerade $x=-\frac{3}{2}$.
The two roots of $p$ add up to $3$.
The two roots of $p$ multiply to $-40$.
$p$ is increasing für every $x>-2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

The two roots sit symmetrically on either side of the axis, so their gap is $\sqrt{\Delta}/|a|$. Compute the discriminant of the given parabola first.

$$\Delta=3^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot(-40)$$

$$3^{2}=9$$

$$\Delta=9-4\cdot 1\cdot(-40)$$

$$\Delta=9+160$$

$$\Delta=169$$

$$|x_{1}-x_{2}|=\frac{\sqrt{169}}{1}$$

$$|x_{1}-x_{2}|=13$$

Solving $x^{2}+3x-40=0$ recovers the roots $-8$ und $5$, which are indeed $13$ apart.

The distance between the two roots is $13$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Wahr

Build the axis von the first two coefficients of the given parabola; the constant $-40$ never enters this formula.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$$

$$a=1,\ b$$

$$a=3$$

$$x=-\frac{3}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$x=-\frac{3}{2}$$

The graph is symmetric in that vertical line, which is also the midpoint of the roots $-8$ und $5$.

The axis is $x=-\frac{3}{2}$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**C.** → Falsch

The sum of the two roots is minus the middle coefficient divided by the leading one.

$$S=-\frac{b}{a}$$

$$S=-\frac{3}{1}$$

$$S=-3$$

The roots themselves are $-8$ und $5$:

$$S=-8+5$$

The claim reports $3$, which drops the minus sign in $-\frac{b}{a}$. The sum is $-3$, not $3$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**D.** → Wahr

The product of the two roots ist das konstante Glied divided by the Leitkoeffizient.

$$P=\frac{c}{a}$$

$$P=\frac{-40}{1}$$

$$P=-40$$

Multiplying the roots confirms the value:

$$P=(-8)\cdot 5$$

The claim reports exactly this product. The two roots multiply to $-40$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**E.** → Falsch

A parabola changes direction exactly once, at its axis $x=-\frac{3}{2}$.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$$

$$a=1$$

$$1>0$$

With a positive stretch the graph falls on everything to the left of the axis und rises on everything to its right.

The half-line $x>-2$ reaches across the axis $x=-\frac{3}{2}$, where the direction changes: on $-2<x<-\frac{3}{2}$ the function is still decreasing.

The claimed half-line is not entirely on the increasing side.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
MATH 7.87.solution_overview:
There is one graph to study, und it is a parabola.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$$

The axis formula fixes the Extrempunkt, while the sum $S$ und the product $P$ of the roots come out of the coefficients mit no equation to solve.

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(-\frac{3}{2},-\frac{169}{4}\right),\qquad S = -3,\qquad P = -40
$$

The discriminant comes out positive, so the graph cuts the $x$-axis twice, once on either side of the Symmetrieachse.

$$
\Delta = 169,\qquad x_{1} = -8,\qquad x_{2} = 5
$$

Die Arme öffnen sich nach oben, daher ist der Extrempunkt der tiefste Punkt des Graphen und der kleinste Wert ist $-\frac{169}{4}$.

MATH 7.88.title: Eine Verschiebung kann eine Parabel nicht abflachen
MATH 7.88.context: The following pair is given: the line $f(x)=-6x+4$ together mit the parabola $g(x)=2x^{2}+3x-2$. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Quadratische Ergänzung liefert $g(x)=2\left(x+\frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}-\frac{25}{8}$.
Some vertical translation of $g$ makes $f-g$ a constant function.
Der Scheitel des Graphen von $g$ ist $\left(-\frac{3}{4},-\frac{25}{8}\right)$.
Die mittlere Änderungsrate von $g$ auf $[0,2]$ entspricht der Steigung von $y=f(x)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Completing the square starts von the axis $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$ und the height there.

$$g(x)=2x^{2}+3x-2$$

$$x=-\frac{3}{2\cdot 2}$$

$$x=-\frac{3}{4}$$

$$g\bigl(-\tfrac{3}{4}\bigr)=2\cdot\tfrac{9}{16}+3\cdot\bigl(-\tfrac{3}{4}\bigr)-2$$

$$g\bigl(-\tfrac{3}{4}\bigr)=\tfrac{9}{8}-\tfrac{9}{4}-2$$

$$g\bigl(-\tfrac{3}{4}\bigr)=-\tfrac{25}{8}$$

Putting the stretch, the shift und the height together recovers the completed square.

$$g(x)=2\bigl(x+\tfrac{3}{4}\bigr)^{2}-\tfrac{25}{8}$$

That is the displayed expression.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Falsch

Translating a graph vertically addiert a fixed number to its formula, which changes the constant term und nothing else, so the $x^{2}$ term of the difference survives untouched.

$$f(x)-g(x)=-2x^{2}-9x+6$$

Shifting $g$ by any real $t$ replaces $g$ by $g+t$ in that difference.

$$f(x)-(g(x)+t)=-2x^{2}-9x+(6-t)$$

The coefficient of $x^{2}$ stays $-2$ für every shift $t$, so the difference remains a genuine parabola und never flattens out.

No vertical translation makes $f-g$ constant.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**C.** → Wahr

The Extrempunkt sits on the axis just computed, so its height is the value of $g$ there.

$$x=-\frac{3}{4}$$

$$g\bigl(-\tfrac{3}{4}\bigr)=-\tfrac{25}{8}$$

$$\text{vertex}=\bigl(-\tfrac{3}{4},-\tfrac{25}{8}\bigr)$$

The Leitkoeffizient $2$ is positive, so this point is the lowest on the graph.

Der Scheitel ist $\bigl(-\frac{3}{4},-\frac{25}{8}\bigr)$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**D.** → Falsch

The average rate of change over an interval ist die Steigung of the chord joining the two endpoint values, so evaluate $g$ at both ends.

$$g(0)=-2$$

$$g(2)=8+6-2$$

$$g(2)=8+6$$

$$g(2)=14$$

$$g(2)=14-2$$

$$g(2)=12$$

$$\frac{g(2)-g(0)}{2-0}=\frac{12-(-2)}{2}$$

$$\frac{g(2)-g(0)}{2-0}=7$$

The line $f(x)=-6x+4$ has slope $-6$, which is a different number.

The chord slope $7$ is not the slope of $f$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**E.** → Wahr

A nested value is computed von the inside outwards: evaluate $g(x)=2x^{2}+3x-2$ at $0$ first, then feed the result into $f(x)=-6x+4$.

$$g(0)=2\cdot 0^{2}+3\cdot 0-2$$

$$0^{2}=0$$

$$g(0)=2\cdot 0+3\cdot 0-2$$

$$g(0)=-2$$

That output now becomes the input of the line.

$$f(-2)=-6\cdot(-2)+4$$

$$f(-2)=12+4$$

$$f(-2)=16$$

Der verschachtelte Wert ist $16$.

$f(g(0))=16$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
MATH 7.88.solution_overview:
Everything starts von the two concrete rules

$$
f(x) = 4 - 6 x,\qquad g(x) = 2 x^{2} + 3 x - 2
$$

The slope, the vertical intercepts und the opening direction all sit in plain view in the coefficients; the arms go upwards.

$$
m = -6,\qquad f(0) = 4,\qquad g(0) = -2,\qquad a = 2
$$

Completing the square moves the Extrempunkt of the parabola into view: the axis comes von the first two coefficients und the height is the value of $g$ there.

$$
g(x) = 2\left(x+\frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}-\frac{25}{8},\qquad \text{vertex} = \left(-\frac{3}{4},-\frac{25}{8}\right)
$$

Comparing the two graphs means solving $f(x)=g(x)$, a quadratic equation whose discriminant reports two real solutions.

$$
f(x)-g(x) = - 2 x^{2} - 9 x + 6,\qquad \Delta = 129
$$

MATH 7.89.title: Geraden durch den Scheitel
MATH 7.89.context: A parabola $g$ has vertex $V$ und nonzero Leitkoeffizient $a$. A line $f$ of slope $m$ is drawn through that same vertex. Es werden keine numerischen Daten angegeben. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Verschwindet $m$, so ist $V$ der einzige gemeinsame Punkt der beiden Graphen.
If $m$ is nonzero, then the graphs have a second common point different von $V$.
Whatever $m$ is, the two graphs are tangent at $V$.
The two graphs always have at least one common point.
Existiert ein zweiter gemeinsamer Punkt, so liegt er genau dann rechts der Achse von $g$, wenn $m$ und $a$ dasselbe Vorzeichen haben.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Put the parabola in Scheitelpunktform around $V=(h,k)$; a line of slope zero through $V$ is simply the horizontal line at that height.

$$g(x)=a(x-h)^{2}+k$$

$$f(x)=k$$

The difference is then a pure square, so the meeting condition has a repeated solution und no other.

$$g(x)-f(x)=a(x-h)^{2}$$

$$g(x)-f(x)= 0$$

$$x$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=h$$

Away von $x=h$ the square is strictly positive und $a\neq 0$, so the difference never returns to zero.

The vertex is the one und only common point in that case.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Wahr

A line through the vertex can sein written using the same shifted variable, und then the difference factors by hand.

$$f(x)=m(x-h)+k$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=a(x-h)^{2}-m(x-h)$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=(x-h)\bigl(a(x-h)-m\bigr)$$

The first factor gives back the vertex; the second one vanishes at an abscissa obtained by dividing the slope by the Leitkoeffizient.

$$a(x-h) = m$$

$$x$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=h+\frac{m}{a}$$

Because $m\neq 0$ und $a\neq 0$ the shift $m/a$ is non-zero, so this second abscissa really is different von $h$.

A second common point appears as soon as the line is tilted.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**C.** → Falsch

Tangency would mean the factored difference has a repeated root at the vertex, so look at the factorisation once more.

$$g(x)-f(x)=(x-h)\bigl(a(x-h)-m\bigr)$$

For $m\neq 0$ the factor $x-h$ occurs only once, so the difference changes sign at $x=h$ und the graphs cross there instead of touching.

$$g(x)=x^{2},\ f(x)$$

$$g(x)= x$$

$$g(x)=g(x)-f(x)$$

$$g(x)=x(x-1)$$

In this example the line through the vertex $(0,0)$ cuts the parabola again at $x=1$, und near the origin the difference is negative on one side und positive on the other.

Only the horizontal choice $m=0$ produces a genuine tangency.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**D.** → Wahr

The line is required to pass through the vertex, so one common point is handed over by the hypothesis itself.

$$f(h)=k$$

$$f(h)=g(h)$$

Both graphs therefore contain the point $V=(h,k)$, whatever the slope $m$ und the Leitkoeffizient $a$ happen to sein.

$$g(x)-f(x)=(x-h)\bigl(a(x-h)-m\bigr)$$

Algebraically the factor $x-h$ is always present in the difference, so the meeting can never sein lost.

At least the vertex is always shared.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**E.** → Wahr

The second meeting was located exactly, so its position relative to the axis $x=h$ is a matter of one sign.

$$x_{2}=h+\frac{m}{a}$$

The point lies to the right of the axis precisely when the added shift is positive, und a quotient of two non-zero numbers is positive exactly when they share a sign.

$$x_{2}>h$$

$$\frac{m}{a}>0$$

$$m\text{ and }a\text{ have the same sign}$$

Opposite signs push the second meeting to the left instead, at the mirrored distance von the axis.

The criterion is exactly the agreement of the two signs.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
MATH 7.89.solution_overview:
Everything is stated für a general parabola, so the reasoning runs on the structure of $ax^{2}+bx+c$ instead of on numbers.

$$
x = -\frac{b}{2a},\qquad \Delta = b^{2}-4ac
$$

Die Symmetrieachse liegt bei $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$; sie folgt aus den ersten beiden Koeffizienten und ignoriert das konstante Glied vollständig. Die Diskriminante zählt die reellen Wurzeln: zwei solange sie positiv ist, eine wenn sie verschwindet und keine, sobald sie negativ wird. Completed-square form puts the Extrempunkt at $(h,k)$, und the sign of $a$ decides whether $k$ is the smallest or the largest value taken.

The line is pinned to the vertex $V$, so one common point is there before any computation starts.

MATH 7.90.title: Eine Parabel mit sich selbst verknüpfen
MATH 7.90.context: A non-constant line $f$ und a parabola $g$ are given. Consider the nested functions $g(g(x))$ und $g(f(g(x)))$. Es werden keine numerischen Daten angegeben. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: The highest power of $x$ in $g(g(x))$ is $x^{4}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $g(f(g(x)))$ is $x^{4}$.
Die höchste Potenz von $x$ in $g(g(x))$ ist $x^{4}$, weil die beiden Potenzen addiert und nicht multipliziert werden.
The nested function $f(f(x))$ is again a non-constant linear function.
For a suitable $g$, the nested function $g(g(x))$ is a quadratic function.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Schreibe $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ mit $a\neq 0$. Nesting substitutes the whole parabola in place of $x$, so the square term gets squared und that is where the top power comes von.

$$g\bigl(g(x)\bigr)=a(ax^{2}+bx+c)^{2}+b(ax^{2}+bx+c)+c$$

Squaring an expression whose highest power is $x^{2}$ reaches $x^{4}$, mit a coefficient that is a product of non-zero numbers.

$$a(ax^{2})^{2}=a^{3}x^{4}$$

The remaining summands only climb to $x^{2}$, so nothing can cancel the $a^{3}x^{4}$ term.

The highest power really is $x^{4}$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Wahr

Schreibe $f(x)=mx+q$ mit $m\neq 0$. Work von the inside out: applying the line to the parabola only rescales it, und then the outer parabola squares the result.

$$f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)=m(ax^{2}+bx+c)+q$$

The Leitkoeffizient here is $ma$, non-zero because the line is non-constant, so the middle stage is still a parabola.

$$g\bigl(f(g(x))\bigr)=a(ma\,x^{2}+\cdots)^{2}+\cdots$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{4}=a(ma)^{2}$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{4}= a^{3}m^{2}\neq 0$$

The triple nesting also tops out at $x^{4}$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**C.** → Falsch

Der Wert $x^{4}$ is right, but the reason offered is not: powers of nested functions multiply, und here $2$ times $2$ happens to agree mit $2$ plus $2$.

$$
2\cdot 2=4,\qquad 2+2 = 4
$$

A single case where the two rules disagree exposes which one is at work: nest the parabola inside the line und count.

$$g\bigl(f(x)\bigr)=a(mx+q)^{2}+b(mx+q)+c$$

The highest power is $x^{2}$, which is $2\cdot 1=2$, not $2+1=3$. Adding the powers is the rule für multiplying two formulas together, not für nesting one inside the other.

The stated justification is the wrong rule, even though the number it produces here is right.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**D.** → Wahr

Schreibe $f(x)=mx+q$ mit $m\neq 0$. Nesting a line inside itself substitutes a first-degree expression into a first-degree formula, so expand und collect.

$$f\bigl(f(x)\bigr)=m(mx+q)+q$$

$$f\bigl(f(x)\bigr)=m^{2}x+q(m+1)$$

The new slope is $m^{2}$, und a square of a non-zero number is non-zero, so the result is a line that is not constant.

$$m\neq 0$$

$$m^{2}>0$$

The double nesting stays a non-constant line.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**E.** → Falsch

For the nesting to collapse to a parabola, the $x^{4}$ term would have to disappear, so look at the coefficient it carries.

$$g\bigl(g(x)\bigr)=a(ax^{2}+bx+c)^{2}+b(ax^{2}+bx+c)+c$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{4}=a^{3}$$

This vanishes only when $a=0$, which is forbidden because $g$ is a parabola; no choice of $b$ or $c$ has any influence on it.

$$a\neq 0$$

$$a^{3}\neq 0$$

The $x^{4}$ term is always there, so the nesting is never a quadratic function.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
MATH 7.90.solution_overview:
Es erscheinen keine Zahlen, daher werden die Behauptungen danach entschieden, was Verschachteln mit der höchsten Potenz von $x$ macht.

$$
f(x) = mx+q,\qquad g(x) = ax^{2}+bx+c,\quad a\neq 0
$$

Verschachteln multipliziert die höchsten Potenzen statt sie zu addieren, daher erreicht das Einsetzen einer Parabel in eine Parabel $x^{4}$, und das Einfügen einer Geraden dazwischen ändert daran nichts.

MATH 7.91.title: Kann eine Gerade eine Parabel einschließen?
MATH 7.91.context: A parabola $g$ mit nonzero Leitkoeffizient $a$ is given together mit a line $f$. Es werden keine numerischen Daten angegeben. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: If $a$ is positive, some line lies strictly below the whole graph of $g$.
If $a$ is positive, some line lies strictly above the whole graph of $g$.
If $a$ is positive, then $g-f$ attains a smallest value für every linear $f$.
If $a$ is negative, some horizontal line lies strictly above the whole graph of $g$.
The graph of $g$ can sein squeezed between two distinct parallel lines over all of $\mathbb{R}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

An upward-opening parabola has a lowest point, und any level below that height gives a line the graph never reaches.

$$g(x)=a(x-h)^{2}+k\ge k\quad\text{for all }x,\qquad a>0$$

Take the horizontal line one unit under the vertex; it is a perfectly legitimate linear function.

$$f(x)=k-1$$

$$g(x)-f(x)\ge 1>0$$

The gap between the two graphs is at least one unit everywhere, so the line stays strictly below the parabola.

Such a line exists, für instance that horizontal one.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Falsch

A line above the whole graph would need $g(x)<f(x)$ für every $x$, so examine the difference far von the origin.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q),\quad a>0$$

The difference is itself an upward-opening parabola, so it has a lowest point und then climbs beyond every bound on both sides.

$$g(x)-f(x)>0\text{ for all }|x|\text{ large enough}$$

The arms of the parabola therefore rise past any line eventually, no matter how steep the line is chosen.

No line can stay above the whole graph when $a>0$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**C.** → Wahr

Subtracting a line changes only the $x$ term und the constant term, so the difference keeps the Leitkoeffizient of $g$.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q),\quad a>0$$

Completing the square exhibits a non-negative square multiplied by a positive number, plus a constant that is actually attained at the vertex.

$$g(x)-f(x)=a(x-h_{d})^{2}+k_{d}\ge k_{d}$$

Der Wert $k_{d}$ depends on the line chosen, but für each line it is a genuine number reached at one abscissa.

The difference attains a smallest value für every linear $f$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**D.** → Wahr

A negative Leitkoeffizient turns the arms downwards, so the vertex is now the highest point of the graph.

$$g(x)=a(x-h)^{2}+k\le k\quad\text{for all }x,\qquad a<0$$

The square is non-negative und $a<0$, so the product is at most zero und the values never climb past the vertex height $k$.

$$f(x)=k+1$$

$$f(x)-g(x)\ge 1>0$$

The horizontal line one unit above the vertex therefore misses the graph entirely und stays above it.

Such a horizontal line exists.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**E.** → Falsch

A strip between two parallel lines has bounded width, so being squeezed inside it would keep the difference to one of those lines bounded.

$$f_{1}(x)=mx+q_{1}$$

$$f_{2}(x)=mx+q_{2}$$

Subtracting the lower line von $g$ leaves a parabola mit the same Leitkoeffizient $a\neq 0$, und such a difference is unbounded.

$$g(x)-f_{1}(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q_{1})$$

For $a>0$ its values exceed $q_{2}-q_{1}$ once $|x|$ is large, und für $a<0$ they fall below the strip instead, so the graph escapes on one side or the other.

A parabola always breaks out of a strip of finite width.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
MATH 7.91.solution_overview:
The parabola arrives already centred on its vertex, so the reasoning stays mit the roles of $a$, $h$ und $k$.

$$g(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}+k$$

Completed-square form puts the Extrempunkt at $(h,k)$, und the sign of $a$ decides whether $k$ is the smallest or the largest value taken. Far out on either side the $x^{2}$ term outgrows every linear term, so the parabola decides who ends up on top.

MATH 7.92.title: Wurzeln über lineare Substitution lesen
MATH 7.92.context: A non-constant line $f$ has slope $m$, und an outer parabola is written $q(y)=Ay^{2}+By+C$ mit nonzero $A$. Set $g(x)=q(f(x))$. Es werden keine numerischen Daten angegeben. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: The function $g$ is a quadratic function.
Every real root of $g$ is a point at which $f$ takes a root value of $q$.
If $q$ has no real roots, then $g$ has no real roots.
Die Wurzeln von $g$ stimmen mit den Wurzeln von $q$ überein.
The coefficient of $x^{2}$ in $g$ equals $A$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Schreibe $f(x)=mx+k$ mit $m\neq 0$. Substituting the line into the outer formula replaces $y$ by a first-degree expression, so expand und collect the powers of $x$.

$$g(x)=A(mx+k)^{2}+B(mx+k)+C$$

$$g(x)=Am^{2}x^{2}+(2Amk+Bm)x+(Ak^{2}+Bk+C)$$

The coefficient of $x^{2}$ is the product $Am^{2}$, und both factors are non-zero: $A$ by hypothesis und $m$ because the line is non-constant.

The substitution produces a genuine quadratic function.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Wahr

The composite is evaluated in two stages, so a zero of the whole thing is a zero produced at the second stage.

$$g(x_{0})=q\bigl(f(x_{0})\bigr)$$

If this number is zero then the value $y_{0}=f(x_{0})$ satisfies $q(y_{0})=0$, so it is one of the roots of $q$.

$$g(x_{0}) = 0$$

$$q(y_{0})$$

$$y_{0}=f(x_{0})$$

The reasoning uses nothing but the definition of nesting, so it applies to every real root of $g$.

Each root of the composite is an abscissa where the line hits a root of $q$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**C.** → Wahr

The composite can only reach values that $q$ itself takes, so a $q$ that never vanishes hands its property straight over.

$$q(y)\neq 0\text{ for every real }y$$

For any real $x$ the number $f(x)$ is real, so $q$ evaluated there is non-zero as well.

$$g(x)=q\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\neq 0\quad\text{for all real }x$$

In terms of discriminants, $q$ having none means its graph misses the horizontal axis, und substituting a line cannot pull it back down.

The composite has no real roots either.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**D.** → Falsch

The roots of the composite are the abscissas whose image under $f$ is a root of $q$, so they are the roots of $q$ pulled back through the line.

$$g(x)=0$$

$$f(x)\text{ is a root of }q$$

One concrete pair shows the shift at once.

$$f(x)=x+1$$

$$q(y)=y^{2}$$

$$g(x)$$

$$q(y)=(x+1)^{2}$$

The only root of $q$ is $0$, while the only root of $g$ is $-1$, so the two sets do not coincide.

The line moves the roots unless it happens to sein the identity.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**E.** → Falsch

The expansion already displays the Leitkoeffizient of the composite, und the slope of the line is squared into it.

$$g(x)=Am^{2}x^{2}+(2Amk+Bm)x+(Ak^{2}+Bk+C)$$

So the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is $Am^{2}$, which equals $A$ only in the special case $m^{2}=1$.

$$m = 2$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{2}$$

$$g(x)= 4A\neq A\text{ unless }A$$

$$g(x)=0$$

Since $A\neq 0$ is assumed, a slope such as $m=2$ genuinely changes the number in front of $x^{2}$.

The Leitkoeffizient is $Am^{2}$, not $A$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

MATH 7.93.title: Gleiche Werte und die Achse

statements: The line $\ell$ passes through the midpoint of $u$ und $v$.

tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Schreibe $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ mit $a\neq 0$. Two equal values give an equation between the coefficients, so subtract the two evaluations und factor.

$$g(u)-g(v)=a(u^{2}-v^{2})+b(u-v)$$

$$g(u)-g(v)=(u-v)\bigl(a(u+v)+b\bigr)$$

The first factor is non-zero because $u$ und $v$ are distinct, so the second one must vanish, which pins down the sum.

$$a(u+v)+b = 0$$

$$a(u+v)+b=\frac{u+v}{2}$$

$$g(u)-g(v)=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

The axis passes through the midpoint of the two abscissas.

**B.** → Falsch

Equal values need not sein zero values, so nothing forces the common value onto the horizontal axis.

$$g(x)=x^{2}$$

$$u=1$$

$$v=-1$$

$$g(1)=1$$

$$g(1)=g(-1)$$

The hypothesis is satisfied mit a common value of $1$, yet the only root of this parabola is $0$, which is neither $u$ nor $v$.

$$g(x) = 0$$

$$x$$

$$g(1)=0$$

Symmetric pairs of abscissas exist at every height, not only at height zero.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**C.** → Wahr

Vertex form makes the symmetry visible: only the distance von the axis enters, through a square.

$$g(x)=a(x-h)^{2}+k$$

$$\ell:\ x=h$$

Evaluating at the two abscissas $h+t$ und $h-t$ squares the same number up to sign, so the two results agree.

$$g(h+t)=at^{2}+k$$

$$g(h-t)=at^{2}+k$$

**D.** → Wahr

Write $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$. The relation derived von $g(u)=g(v)$ involved no data beyond the coefficients, so read it again.

$$(u-v)\bigl(a(u+v)+b\bigr)=0,\quad u\neq v$$

$$u+v=-\frac{b}{a}$$

Whatever pair of distinct abscissas mit equal values one starts von, its sum is this one number, which is twice the abscissa of the axis.

The sum is fixed by $a$ und $b$ alone.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**E.** → Wahr

The Symmetrieachse always exists, und it supplies such a pair für free.

$$h=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$u=h+1$$

$$v=h-1$$

$$g(h+1)=a+k$$

$$g(h+1)=g(h-1)$$

The construction only needs $a\neq 0$, which is part of being a quadratic function, so it works für every $g$ of this kind.

Such a pair can always sein produced.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

MATH 7.94.title: Ein Geradenbüschel und zwei Tangenten
MATH 7.94.context: A fixed parabola $g(x)=x^{2}-4x+6$ is compared mit the family of lines $f_t(x)=t(x-1)+2$ obtained as the real parameter $t$ varies. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Every line of the family passes through one und the same point.

tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

The parameter multiplies the bracket $x-1$, so it loses all its influence wherever that bracket vanishes.

$$f_{t}(1)=t\cdot 0+2$$

$$f_{t}(1)=2$$

Every member of the family therefore reaches the height $2$ at the abscissa $1$, whatever the slope.

$$t = 0$$

$$f_{0}(x)$$

$$f_{t}(1)=2$$

$$t=3$$

$$f_{3}(x)$$

$$t=3x-1$$

**B.** → Wahr

Touching at a single point means $g(x)=f_{t}(x)$ has a repeated solution, so collect the terms und set the discriminant to zero.

$$x^{2}-4x+6-t(x-1)-2=x^{2}-(4+t)x+(4+t)$$

$$\Delta(t)=t(4+t)$$

$$t(4+t) = 0$$

$$t$$

$$\Delta(t)=0\text{ or }t$$

$$\Delta(t)=-4$$

The first gives the horizontal line $y=2$ touching at the vertex $(2,2)$, the second the line $y=-4x+6$ touching at $(0,6)$.

There are exactly two such slopes.

**C.** → Wahr

A member misses the parabola exactly when the discriminant is negative, so study the sign of the product just obtained.

$$\Delta(t)=t(4+t)$$

A product of two factors is negative when they have opposite signs, which happens strictly between the two roots.

$$-4<t<0$$

$$\Delta(t)<0$$

$$t = -2$$

$$t=\Delta(-2)$$

$$\Delta(t)=(-2)\cdot 2$$

$$\Delta(t)=-4$$

$$-4<0$$

The line $y=-2x+4$ therefore shares no point mit the curve.

Slopes in that window make the line miss the parabola.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**D.** → Falsch

Two distinct meetings need a strictly positive discriminant, und the discriminant has already been factored.

$$\Delta(t)=t(4+t)$$

It vanishes at $t=0$ und $t=-4$, where the line only touches the curve, und it is negative in between, where nothing is shared.

$$t = -2$$

$$\Delta$$

$$\Delta(t)=-4$$

$$-4<0$$

$$t=0$$

Some slopes give one meeting und some give none, so two distinct meetings do not always occur.

The claim fails für a whole interval of slopes.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**E.** → Falsch

The fixed point of the pencil was found to sein $(1,2)$, so test whether the parabola reaches that height there.

$$g(1)=1^{2}-4+6$$

$$1^{2}=1$$

$$g(1)=1-4+6$$

$$g(1)=1-4$$

$$g(1)=-3$$

$$g(1)=-3+6$$

$$g(1)=3$$

The parabola is at height $3$ while the fixed point sits at height $2$, so the point lies strictly below the curve.

$$\text{vertex of }g=(2,2),\qquad g(1)=3\neq 2$$

That position is exactly what makes the two tangent lines und the window of missing lines possible.

MATH 7.94.solution_overview:
A fixed parabola $g(x)=x^{2}-4x+6$ is compared mit the family of lines $f_t(x)=t(x-1)+2$ obtained as the real parameter $t$ varies.

Rekonstruiere hier einmal die gemeinsame Gerade und Parabel; jeder Buchstabe prüft nur die in seiner Behauptung genannte Zusatzrechnung.

$g-f_t=x^{2}-(4+t)x+(4+t)$ mit discriminant $t(4+t)$: two tangent slopes, und no meeting in between.

$$
f_{t}(1) = t\cdot 0+2 = 2
$$

$$
t = 0\implies f_{0}(x) = 2,\qquad t = 3\implies f_{3}(x) = 3x-1
$$

$$
x^{2}-4x+6-t(x-1)-2 = x^{2}-(4+t)x+(4+t) = 0
$$

MATH 7.95.title: Die Parabel seitlich verschieben
MATH 7.95.context: A fixed line $f(x)=2x-1$ is compared mit the family of parabolas $g_r(x)=(x-r)^{2}-4$ obtained as the real shift $r$ varies. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Es gibt genau eine Verschiebung, für die die Gerade die Parabel berührt.

The Symmetrieachse of $g_r$ moves as $r$ changes.

**A.** → Wahr

The family moves a fixed parabola left und right, und tangency means $g_{r}(x)=f(x)$ has a repeated solution.

$$(x-r)^{2}-4-(2x-1)=x^{2}-(2r+2)x+(r^{2}-3)$$

$$(x-r)^{2}-4-(2x-1)=0$$

$$\Delta(r)=(2r+2)^{2}-4(r^{2}-3)$$

$$\Delta(r)=8r+16$$

The squares in $r$ cancel, so the condition is a first-degree equation mit one solution.

$$8r+16 = 0$$

$$r$$

$$\Delta(r)=-2$$

At that shift the difference becomes $(x+1)^{2}$, a perfect square touching zero once.

Exactly one shift makes the line tangent.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Wahr

Missing each other means a negative discriminant, und the discriminant just computed increases steadily mit the shift.

$$\Delta(r)=8r+16$$

$$r<-2$$

$$\Delta(r)<0$$

Taking $r=-3$, für instance, leaves no real solution:

$$\Delta(r)=\Delta(-3)$$

$$\Delta(r)=-24+16$$

$$\Delta(r)=-8$$

$$-8<0$$

Sufficiently negative shifts separate the graphs.

**C.** → Falsch

The formula is already in Scheitelpunktform, so the Extrempunkt can sein read straight off it.

$$g_{r}(x) = (x-r)^{2}-4$$

$$\text{vertex}=(r,-4)$$

$$r = 0$$

$$\text{vertex }(0,-4)$$

$$r=5$$

$$\text{vertex }(5,-4)$$

The vertex height stays $-4$ für every shift.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**D.** → Wahr

The Symmetrieachse is the vertical line through the vertex, und Scheitelpunktform puts the vertex at abscissa $r$.

$$g_{r}(x) = (x-r)^{2}-4$$

$$\ell:\ x=r$$

The mirrored values confirm it, since only the distance von $r$ enters the square.

$$g_{r}(r+t)=t^{2}-4$$

$$g_{r}(r+t)=g_{r}(r-t)$$

Changing $r$ therefore drags the axis along mit the whole graph.

The axis moves exactly as much as the shift.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**E.** → Falsch

The crossing mit the vertical coordinate axis is the value at $x=0$, so substitute und see whether the shift survives.

$$g_{r}(0)=(0-r)^{2}-4$$

$$g_{r}(0)=r^{2}-4$$

The result depends on $r$, und two members already disagree.

$$r = 0$$

$$g_{0}(0)$$

$$g_{r}(0)=-4$$

$$r=3$$

$$g_{3}(0)$$

$$r=5$$

Sliding a parabola sideways changes the height at which it passes the $y$-axis.

The family crosses the $y$-axis at different points.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
MATH 7.95.solution_overview:
A fixed line $f(x)=2x-1$ is compared mit the family of parabolas $g_r(x)=(x-r)^{2}-4$ obtained as the real shift $r$ varies.

Rekonstruiere hier einmal die gemeinsame Gerade und Parabel; jeder Buchstabe prüft nur die in seiner Behauptung genannte Zusatzrechnung.

$g_r-f=x^{2}-(2r+2)x+(r^{2}-3)$ mit discriminant $8r+16$: tangency at $r=-2$.

$$
(x-r)^{2}-4-(2x-1) = x^{2}-(2r+2)x+(r^{2}-3) = 0
$$

$$

MATH 7.96.title: Rekonstruktion aus Scheitel und einem Punkt
MATH 7.96.context: The line $f$ has slope $-3$ und passes through the point $(1,2)$. The quadratic $g$ has Leitkoeffizient $2$ und its vertex at $(2,-8)$. Recover both formulas, then judge the statements. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Die Wurzeln von $g$ sind $0$ und $4$.
Die Graphen von $f$ und $g$ treffen sich in einem Punkt der $y$-Achse.
Das Anpassen von $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ erzwingt $A=\frac{2}{9}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

A slope und one point determine a line, und the point-slope shape is the quickest route to its formula.

$$f(x)=-3(x-1)+2$$

$$f(x)=-3x+3+2$$

$$f(x)=-3x+5$$

The check is immediate: the slope is $-3$ und the value at $x=1$ is $2$, as required.

$$f(1)=-3+5$$

$$f(1)=2$$

The recovered formula is exactly the one claimed.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Wahr

A Leitkoeffizient together mit a vertex determines a parabola, und Scheitelpunktform assembles it directly.

$$g(x)=2(x-2)^{2}-8$$

$$g(x)=2(x^{2}-4x+4)-8$$

$$g(x)=2x^{2}-8x$$

The constant terms cancel. Checking against the vertex: the axis is at

$$x=-\frac{-8}{2\cdot 2}$$

$$x=-\frac{-8}{4}$$

$$x=2$$

 und the value there is $8-16=-8$.

The expanded formula matches the claim.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**C.** → Wahr

With no constant term the recovered formula factors at sight, so the roots need no quadratic formula.

$$g(x)=2x^{2}-8x$$

$$g(x)=2x(x-4)$$

A product vanishes exactly when one of its factors does, und the factor $2$ never does.

$$2x(x-4) = 0$$

$$x$$

$$g(x)=0\text{ or }x$$

$$g(x)=4$$

The midpoint of the two roots is $2$, which is the Symmetrieachse found von the vertex, so the two computations agree.

Die Wurzeln sind $0$ und $4$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**D.** → Falsch

A common point on the vertical coordinate axis would mean the two functions agree at $x=0$, so evaluate both there.

$$f(0)=5$$

$$g(0)=0$$

The heights differ, so $x=0$ is not a meeting abscissa. Solving the meeting equation confirms where the graphs actually cross.

$$2x^{2}-8x = -3x+5$$

$$h=2x^{2}-5x-5$$

$$h=0$$

$$\Delta=25+40$$

$$\Delta= 65$$

$$x$$

$$\Delta=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{65}}{4}$$

Neither of these abscissas is $0$, since the constant term $-5$ of that equation is non-zero.

The graphs do meet twice, but never on the $y$-axis.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**E.** → Wahr

Only the term $Af(x)^{2}$ can supply an $x^{2}$, so square the recovered line und compare that coefficient mit the one in $g$.

$$f(x)^{2}=(-3x+5)^{2}$$

$$f(x)^{2}=9x^{2}-30x+25$$

$$9A = 2$$

$$A$$

$$f(x)^{2}=\frac{2}{9}$$

The division is legitimate because the slope $-3$ is non-zero, und no other value of $A$ can reproduce the coefficient $2$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

MATH 7.97.title: Achsenabstand, Vieta und verschachtelte Reihenfolge
MATH 7.97.context: A concrete line $f$ und a concrete parabola $g$ are supplied: $f(x)=3x-7$, $g(x)=x^{2}-5x+2$. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Quadratische Ergänzung liefert $g(x)=\left(x-\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{17}{4}$.
At the axis of $g$ the gap $f-g$ equals $\frac{19}{4}$.
Nach Vieta ist die Summe der Wurzeln von $g$ gleich $-5$.
The graphs of $f$ und $g$ meet at two distinct points.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Die quadratische Ergänzung isoliert die Achsenverschiebung aus der Hälfte des mittleren Koeffizienten und stellt dann die Konstante wieder her, sodass die umgeschriebene Formel dem ursprünglichen Polynom entspricht.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-5x+2$$

Halbiere den mittleren Koeffizienten des monischen quadratischen Faktors.

$$\frac{b}{2a}=-\frac{5}{2}$$

$$\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2=\frac{25}{4}$$

Die Achsenverschiebung ist das Gegenteil dieses halbierten Koeffizienten.

$$h=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$h=\frac{5}{2}$$

Werte die ursprüngliche Vorschrift an der Achse aus, um die Höhe nach quadratischer Ergänzung abzulesen.

$$g\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)=-\frac{17}{4}$$

Setze Streckung, Verschiebung und Höhe zusammen.

$$g(x)=\left(x-\frac{5}{2}\right)^2-\frac{17}{4}$$

Das stimmt mit der behaupteten Form nach quadratischer Ergänzung überein.

$$g(x)=\left(x-\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{17}{4}$$

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Wahr

The vertical gap between the two graphs at a given abscissa is the difference of the two heights there, so locate the axis of the parabola first und then evaluate both models on it.

$$x=\frac{5}{2}$$

$$f\bigl(\tfrac{5}{2}\bigr)=3\cdot\tfrac{5}{2}-7$$

$$f\bigl(\tfrac{5}{2}\bigr)=\tfrac{1}{2}$$

$$g\bigl(\tfrac{5}{2}\bigr)=-\tfrac{17}{4}$$

Subtracting the parabola height von the line height gives the gap.

$$\tfrac{1}{2}-\bigl(-\tfrac{17}{4}\bigr)=\tfrac{2}{4}+\tfrac{17}{4}$$

$$\tfrac{1}{2}-\bigl(-\tfrac{17}{4}\bigr)=\tfrac{19}{4}$$

The gap is $\frac{19}{4}$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**C.** → Falsch

The sum of the two roots is minus the middle coefficient divided by the leading one. For $g(x)=x^{2}-5x+2$,

$$S=-\frac{b}{a}$$

$$S=-\frac{-5}{1}$$

$$S=5$$

The claim reports $-5$, which keeps the minus sign in front of $b$ instead of cancelling it against the minus already present in $-5$. Die Summe der Wurzeln ist $5$, nicht $-5$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**D.** → Falsch

Nesting is not symmetric: feeding the line into the parabola need not agree mit feeding the parabola into the line, so each order has to sein computed on its own.

$$f(0)=-7$$

$$g(-7)=49+35+2$$

$$g(-7)=49+35$$

$$g(-7)=84$$

$$g(-7)=84+2$$

$$g(-7)=86$$

$$g(0)=2$$

$$f(2)=6-7$$

$$f(2)=-1$$

The two orders give $86$ und $-1$, which are different numbers.

$g(f(0))\neq f(g(0))$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**E.** → Wahr

The abscissas where the graphs meet solve $g(x)=f(x)$, so bring the line over und read the discriminant.

$$x^{2}-5x+2-(3x-7)=x^{2}-8x+9$$

$$x^{2}-5x+2-(3x-7)=0$$

$$\Delta=(-8)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 9$$

$$\Delta=64-36$$

$$\Delta=28$$

A strictly positive discriminant makes the square root a genuine positive number, so the quadratic formula returns two different real abscissas.

$$x=\frac{8\pm\sqrt{28}}{2}$$

$$x=4\pm\sqrt{7}$$

Both values are real und they differ by $2\sqrt{7}$, so the line cuts the parabola in two separate points.

The graphs meet at two distinct points.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
MATH 7.97.solution_overview:
The stem names a line und a parabola,

$$
f(x) = 3 x - 7,\qquad g(x) = x^{2} - 5 x + 2
$$

The Extrempunkt is worth having in hand: the Symmetrieachse is read off the first two coefficients, und evaluating $g$ there supplies the height.

$$
g(x) = \left(x-\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{17}{4},\qquad \text{vertex} = \left(\frac{5}{2},-\frac{17}{4}\right)
$$

Coefficients alone settle the sum $S$ und the product $P$ of the roots of $g$, und the sign of its discriminant tells how many of those roots are real.

$$
S = 5,\qquad P = 2,\qquad \Delta_{g} = 17
$$

Wherever the two graphs touch, the difference $f-g$ is zero; that difference is quadratic und its discriminant leaves two crossings.

$$
f(x)-g(x) = - x^{2} + 8 x - 9,\qquad \Delta = 28
$$

MATH 7.E01.title: Lichtraumprofil — Schnittpunkte und eine Sehne
MATH 7.E01.context: The figure shows a **solid brown parabola** $g$ und a **dashed green line** $f$. No formulas are printed. Reason von the ticks, crossings, und relative heights only. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Das Produkt der beiden Schnittabszissen der Graphen ist negativ.

**A.** → Wahr

Meetings of a line und a parabola are the real zeros of their height difference, so recover both traces von the ticks und subtract.

**B.** → Falsch

The solid curve turns on the vertical axis, at the unique trough of an even downward parabola. Compare the two heights at that common abscissa.

$$f(0)=2$$

**C.** → Wahr

Use the shared rules recovered in the overview.

$$g(x)-f(x)=-x^{2}+x+2$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=-(x-2)(x+1)$$

The two real meetings are therefore $x=-1$ und $x=2$. Only the first of those is strictly negative.

$$x=-1$$

$$-1<0$$

$$x=2$$

$$2>0$$

A meeting to the right of the origin does not count toward the left-hand tally, und a quadratic difference has no third real zero.

A single negative abscissa is exactly one meeting to the left of the origin.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**D.** → Falsch

The solid curve meets the horizontal axis at $x=\pm 2$. On the open interval between those crossings the midpoint $x=0$ already compares the two traces.

$$g(x)=-x^{2}+4$$

$$f(x)=-x+2$$

$$g(0)=4$$

$$f(0)=2$$

Brown stays above green at the vertex, und an upward gap at the axis of a downward parabola cannot flip between the two roots.

$$4>2$$

The solid curve is above the dashed line on that interval, not below it.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**E.** → Falsch

A chord joining the two axis crossings of $g$ is the unique line through $(\pm 2,0)$, which is the horizontal axis itself.

$$g(\pm 2) = 0$$

$$y=0$$

MATH 7.E05.title: Verschiebbare Steigungsschar — wann Tangentialität eintritt

$$g(x)-f_t(x)=x^{2}-tx+1$$

$$\Delta=0$$

$$t=\pm 2$$

$$x^{2}=-1\text{ is impossible in }\mathbb{R}$$

**D.** → Falsch

$$t=3$$

$$\Delta=9-4$$

$$\Delta=5$$

$$5>0$$

$$t=3$$

$$3>2$$

$$\text{two real meetings}$$

$$g(x)=x^{2}+1$$

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$x=0$$

$$

The parabola is fixed und the line slides through the origin as the slope $t$ varies.

$$

$$

$$g(x)-f_t(x)=x^{2}-tx+1$$

The discriminant of that family is a quadratic in the parameter, und its sign sorts the geometry into miss, tangency, und two crossings.

$$

The axis of $g$ is read von its own coefficients und never sees $t$.

$$

$$

MATH 7.E06.title: Rekonstruktion aus Scheitel und einem Punkt

**B.** → Wahr

**C.** → Wahr

Vertex form mit the given Extrempunkt und the given point $(0,5)$ forces stretch $a=2$. Then evaluate at $x=1$ und at the reflected input $x=3$.

$$g(x)=2(x-2)^{2}-3$$

$$g(1)=2(1-2)^{2}-3$$

$$g(1)=-1$$

The same identity $g(2+t)=g(2-t)$ mit $t=1$ pairs $x=1$ mit $x=3$, so the two heights cannot differ.

$$g(2+1)=-1$$

Both heights equal $-1$, matching the equal distance von the axis $x=2$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**D.** → Falsch

The vertex is the given Extrempunkt $(2,-3)$. Its height is already negative, so it does not lie above the axis, und $(2,-3)$ itself is a given point of negative height.

$$g(2)=-3$$

$$-3<0$$

The other given point $(0,5)$ does have positive height, but that cannot rescue the vertex.

$$(2,-3)\text{ is below }y=0$$

Opening upwards mit a negative vertex height is the usual picture of a trough below the axis, not a peak above it.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**E.** → Falsch

The claimed rule is Scheitelpunktform mit stretch $1$ instead of the $a=2$ that hits $(0,5)$. Check it against that given point.

$$(0-2)^{2}-3=1\neq 5$$

$$g(x)=2(x-2)^{2}-3$$

Die Aussage ist falsch.
MATH 7.E06.solution_overview:
A vertex und a second point determine a unique parabola of the completed-square shape $a(x-h)^{2}+k$, und the stem already names both $h$ und $k$.

$$g(x)=a(x-2)^{2}-3$$

The extra point $(0,5)$ fixes the stretch $a$. Substitute $x=0$ und solve the one-step equation.

$$a(0-2)^{2}-3=5$$

$$
4a = 8,\qquad a = 2
$$

The rebuilt rule is therefore

$$
g(x) = 2(x-2)^{2}-3 = 2x^{2}-8x+5
$$

The axis is the vertical line through the given vertex, und evaluating at the two symmetric inputs $x=0$ und $x=4$ gives the same height $5$.

$$
\text{axis}:\ x = 2,\qquad g(0) = 5,\qquad g(4) = 5
$$

The vertex height $-3$ lies below the horizontal axis, so the Extrempunkt is a trough rather than a peak above $y=0$. Because $a=2>0$ the arms open upwards, matching the stem.

$$
\mathrm{ver} = \left(2,-3\right),\qquad a = 2>0
$$

MATH 7.E07.title: Gerade in einem Quadrat — Achse der anderen Ordnung
MATH 7.E07.context: Let $f(x)=x+1$ und $g(x)=x^{2}$. Study the nested rules $g(f(x))$ und $f(g(x))$. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: The nested rule $g(f(x))$ expands to a perfect square, so its vertex lies on the horizontal axis.
The nested rule $f(g(x))$ has the same Symmetrieachse as $g$.
The two nested rules are identical as functions.
The nested rules $g(f(x))$ und $f(g(x))$ have the same vertex.
The highest power appearing in $f(g(x))$ is $x^{3}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Nesting the line inside the square substitutes a first-degree expression für $x$, so expand the square.

$$g(f(x))=(x+1)^{2}$$

$$g(f(x))=x^{2}+2x+1$$

A perfect square $(x+1)^{2}$ vanishes at $x=-1$ und is never negative, so the vertex sits on the horizontal axis.

$$g(f(-1))=0$$

A vertex on the axis is the geometric form of a double root at $x=-1$, visible as the square $(x+1)^{2}$.

The nesting is a perfect square whose vertex lies on the axis.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Wahr

In this order the square is computed first und the line is applied afterwards, which merely shifts the values vertically.

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$$

A vertical shift leaves the Symmetrieachse untouched: both $x^{2}$ und $x^{2}+1$ turn on the vertical coordinate axis.

$$x=-\frac{0}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$x=-\frac{0}{2}$$

$$x=0$$

An operation performed on the values can only stretch or slide the graph vertically, which cannot move a vertical axis.

The composite $f(g(x))$ has the same axis as $g$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**C.** → Falsch

The two expansions already differ by the middle term $2x$. A concrete input makes the gap visible.

$$g(f(x))=(x+1)^{2}$$

$$g(f(x))=x^{2}+2x+1$$

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$$

At $x=1$ one composite equals $4$ und the other equals $2$. Equal highest powers do not make the maps identical.

$$g(f(1)) = 4\neq 2$$

$$f(g(x))=f(g(1))$$

Equal highest powers do not make two polynomials the same function: the linear term $2x$ is present in one expansion und absent in the other.

The nested rules are not the same function.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**D.** → Falsch

Die quadratische Ergänzung isoliert die Achsenverschiebung aus der Hälfte des mittleren Koeffizienten und stellt dann die Konstante wieder her, sodass die umgeschriebene Formel dem ursprünglichen Polynom entspricht.

$$g(x)=x^{2}$$

Halbiere den mittleren Koeffizienten des monischen quadratischen Faktors.

$$\frac{b}{2a}=0$$

$$\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2=0$$

Die Achsenverschiebung ist das Gegenteil dieses halbierten Koeffizienten.

$$h=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$h=0$$

Werte die ursprüngliche Vorschrift an der Achse aus, um die Höhe nach quadratischer Ergänzung abzulesen.

$$g(0)=(0)^{2}+(0)\cdot(0)+(0)$$

$$g(0)=0+(0)+(0)$$

$$g(0)=0$$

Setze Streckung, Verschiebung und Höhe zusammen.

$$g(x)=x^{2}$$

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**E.** → Falsch

A line applied after a square can only stretch und shift the values, so the highest power stays $x^{2}$. Nesting multiplies highest powers instead of adding them.

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$$

The product of the degrees is $1\cdot 2=2$, not $1+2=3$. No $x^{3}$ term is produced.

$$\text{highest power }x^{2},\text{ not }x^{3}$$

Take the inner square $g(x)=x^{2}$ of degree $2$ und the outer line of degree $1$: the composite has degree $2$, mit no $x^{3}$ term to invent.

The highest power in $f(g(x))$ is $x^{2}$, not $x^{3}$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
MATH 7.E07.solution_overview:
The stem names a line und a parabola, und the letters ask für both nestings, so expand each composition once und keep the two polynomials.

$$
f(x) = x+1,\qquad g(x) = x^{2}
$$

Feeding the line into the parabola squares the whole linear expression.

$$
g(f(x)) = (x+1)^{2} = x^{2}+2x+1
$$

Feeding the parabola into the line only shifts the square by a constant.

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$$

Both results are quadratic — nesting a line mit a parabola cannot raise the highest power above $x^{2}$ — but the coefficients differ, so the two nested rules are different functions. A single test point already separates them.

$$
g(f(1)) = 4,\qquad f(g(1)) = 2
$$

The highest power in $f(g(x))$ is $x^{2}$, not $x^{3}$. Substituting a degree-$1$ rule into a degree-$2$ rule (or the other way around) multiplies those degrees und leaves a quadratic.

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1,\qquad \text{highest power }x^{2}\text{ (not }x^{3})$$

MATH 7.E08.title: Skaliertes Produkt — Vieta mit Leitkoeffizient $2$
MATH 7.E08.context: Let $g(x)=2(x-1)(x-5)$. Decide each claim von the factored form. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Die Summe der Wurzeln ist $6$, daher ist die Symmetrieachse $x=3$.
Die Scheitelhöhe beträgt $-8$, das Doppelte der Höhe, die man ohne den Leitkoeffizienten $2$ erhielte.
The values $g(0)$ und $g(6)$ agree, so $x=0$ und $x=6$ sit equally far von the axis.
Das konstante Glied equals $10$, und the product of the roots is $5$.
Expanded, the middle coefficient equals $-10$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

A product $2(x-1)(x-5)$ vanishes precisely where a factor vanishes, so the roots are $1$ und $5$ regardless of the leading $2$.

$$x=1$$

$$
x=5,\qquad 1+5 = 6
$$

The axis is the midpoint of those two roots, which is also $x=-b/(2a)$ after expanding.

$$x=\frac{1+5}{2}$$

$$x=\frac{6}{2}$$

$$x=3$$

A Leitkoeffizient stretches the graph vertically und does not move the zeros, so the axis is still the midpoint of $1$ und $5$.

The sum of the roots is $6$ und the axis is $x=3$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Wahr

The vertex sits on the axis $x=3$, the midpoint of the roots $1$ und $5$. Evaluate the factored form there, keeping the leading $2$.

$$g(3)=2(3-1)(3-5)$$

$$g(3)=2\cdot 2\cdot(-2)$$

$$g(3)=-8$$

Dropping the leading $2$ would have produced $-4$, half of the true height. The stretch doubles that dropped-leading trap.

$$g(3)=-4\neq -8$$

The vertex height is $-8$, twice the height one would get by dropping the leading $2$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**C.** → Wahr

The axis bisects the roots $1$ und $5$, so it is $x=3$. The inputs $0$ und $6$ sit three units on either side, hence a parabola takes the same value at both.

$$g(0)=2(-1)(-5)$$

$$g(0)=10$$

$$g(6)=2(5)(1)$$

$$g(6)=10$$

Symmetry about $x=3$ is $g(3+t)=g(3-t)$. The pair $t=3$ recovers $x=0$ und $x=6$ mit a common height $10$.

$$g(3+3)=g(3-3)$$

$$g(3+3)=10$$

Those two heights agree, so $x=0$ und $x=6$ sit equally far von the axis.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**D.** → Wahr

Das konstante Glied is the value at the origin, which the factored form gives without a full expansion.

$$g(0)=2(-1)(-5)$$

$$g(0)=10$$

Vieta's product is that constant over the Leitkoeffizient, which is also the product of the named roots.

$$P=\frac{10}{2}$$

$$P=5$$

$$P=1\cdot 5$$

The product of the roots is independent of the leading $2$ once it is cancelled in $c/a$, which is why $P=5$ matches $1\cdot 5$.

Constant term $10$ und product of roots $5$ both match.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**E.** → Falsch

Expand the inner product first, then distribute the leading $2$. The middle coefficient comes von the sum of the roots, scaled by $-2$.

$$(x-1)(x-5)=x^{2}-6x+5$$

$$2(x^{2}-6x+5)=2x^{2}-12x+10$$

The trap $-10$ is what one would get von $2\times(-5)$ if the inner sum of roots had been taken to sein $5$ instead of $6$.

$$2(x^{2}-6x+5)=-12\neq -10$$

The middle coefficient of $a(x-r)(x-s)$ is

$$-a(r+s)=-2\cdot 6$$

$$-a(r+s)=-12$$

not $-2\cdot 5$.

The middle coefficient is $-12$, not $-10$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
MATH 7.E08.solution_overview:
The parabola is already factored, so the roots can sein read off the brackets before any expansion.

$$g(x)=2(x-1)(x-4)$$

Die Nullstellen sind $x=1$ und $x=4$. Their midpoint is the axis, und Vieta will confirm the same midpoint after expanding.

$$
x = 1,\qquad x = 4,\qquad x = \frac{5}{2}
$$

Expanding once produces the three coefficients every later letter needs.

$$g(x)=2x^{2}-10x+8$$

The middle coefficient is $-10$ und the constant term is $8$. The vertex height is the value of $g$ on the axis, not the constant term und not $-4$.

$$
g\left(\frac{5}{2}\right) = 2\cdot\frac{25}{4}-10\cdot\frac{5}{2}+8 = -\frac{9}{2}
$$

$$
S = 5,\qquad P = 4,\qquad \Delta_{g} = 36,\qquad \mathrm{ver} = \left(\frac{5}{2},-\frac{9}{2}\right)
$$

Because the Leitkoeffizient $2$ is positive the arms open upwards und this vertex is a trough.

MATH 7.E09.title: Parabel-Figur, Geraden-Tabelle — kombinierte Ablesung
MATH 7.E09.context: The figure shows an unknown parabola $g$ (solid brown; no formula). Separately, the table lists an unknown line $\ell$ at four inputs. Use the figure für claims about $g$ und the table für claims about $\ell$. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Die beiden Achsenschnitte der durchgezogenen Kurve sind Gegensätze zueinander.
Der Extrempunkt der durchgezogenen Kurve liegt $4$ Einheiten unter der horizontalen Achse.
Die ersten Differenzen der tabellierten Höhen sind konstant $2$, und die zweiten Differenzen verschwinden daher; der Interpolationsgrad ist $1$.
A line of slope $2$ through $(0,1)$ matches every tabled point.
At the solid curve's right-hand axis crossing, the tabled height equals $5$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Count the brown meetings mit the horizontal axis und read their abscissas von the ticks. The trough sits on the vertical axis, so the two crossings must sein opposites.

$$x=-2$$

$$x=2$$

Those two numbers are opposites of each other, matching the visual symmetry of the trough about the vertical axis. Rebuilding von the ticks gives

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4$$

whose roots are exactly $\pm 2$.

The two axis crossings are opposites.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Wahr

The marked trough sits on the vertical axis. Its height on the vertical scale is $-4$, four units below the horizontal axis.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4$$

$$g(0)=-4$$

An even upward parabola turns at the origin, und that turning height ist das konstante Glied.

$$-4<0$$

An even upward parabola $x^{2}-4$ turns at the origin, so the trough height ist das konstante Glied, already $-4$ on the vertical scale.

$$x=-\frac{0}{2}$$

$$x=0$$

$$g(0)=-4$$

The Extrempunkt lies $4$ units below the axis.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**C.** → Wahr

Form neighbouring gaps of the $\ell$-row; the table does not print them. The four heights are $1,3,5,7$.

$$
3-1=2,\qquad 5-3 = 2,\qquad 7-5 = 2
$$

Constant first difference $2$ forces vanishing second differences, which is the hallmark of degree $1$.

$$\Delta_{2}:\ 0,\ 0$$

A quadratic on unit spacing would freeze only at the second layer, mit a nonzero constant. Vanishing second differences drop the degree to $1$.

$$2a=0$$

$$a=0$$

The interpolating degree is $1$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**D.** → Wahr

For unit spacing, a constant first difference ist die Steigung. The tabled height at $x=0$ is the intercept.

$$m=2$$

$$\ell(0)=1$$

$$\ell(x)=2x+1$$

Checking the remaining columns recovers the listed heights: $2\cdot 1+1=3$, $2\cdot 2+1=5$, $2\cdot 3+1=7$.

$$\ell(1)=3$$

$$\ell(2)=5$$

$$\ell(3)=7$$

Any other pair von the table gives the same slope: $(7-1)/(3-0)=2$, so the interpolating line is unique.

That line reproduces the whole table.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**E.** → Wahr

The right-hand brown axis crossing sits at $x=2$ on the figure, because $g(x)=x^{2}-4$ vanishes there. The same abscissa is a column of the table.

$$g(2)=0$$

$$\ell(x)=2x+1$$

$$\ell(2)=5$$

The two data sources are independent: the ticks name the abscissa $x=2$, und the table names the height $\ell(2)=5$ at that same input.

The figure supplies the abscissa; the table supplies the height at that same input. The tabled height at that crossing is $5$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
MATH 7.E09.solution_overview:
Two media sit side by side: a figure für the unknown parabola $g$ und a four-point table für the unknown line $\ell$. Recover each model once, then reuse the recovered rules.

$$
g(x) = x^{2}-4,\qquad \ell(x) = 2x+1
$$

The solid brown curve is an upward trough on the vertical axis, meeting the horizontal axis at $x=\pm 2$. Completing the square is immediate.

$$
g(x) = x^{2}-4,\qquad \mathrm{ver} = \left(0,-4\right),\qquad x = \pm 2
$$

The vertex lies $4$ units below the horizontal axis. The Leitkoeffizient $1$ sends the arms upwards.

$$
a = 1>0,\qquad S = 0,\qquad P = -4,\qquad \Delta_{g} = 16
$$

The tabled heights form an arithmetic sequence: each step of the input raises the output by $2$.

$$\ell:\ 1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7\qquad \mathrm{fir}:\ 2,\ 2,\ 2$$

Constant first differences of $2$ mit unit spacing mean slope $2$, und the value at $x=0$ is the intercept $1$, recovering $\ell(x)=2x+1$.

$$
m = 2,\qquad \ell(0) = 1
$$

MATH 7.E10.title: Kai-Kran — Streckung von einem genannten Scheitel
MATH 7.E10.context: A dock crane's clearance is modelled by a parabola $g$ that öffnet sich nach unten, turns at $(1,6)$, und meets the deck $y=0$ at $x=-1$ und $x=3$. A linear sensor path $f$ passes through $(0,2)$ mit slope $-1$. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: The rule für $g$ is $g(x)=-(x+1)(x-3)$, und this unscaled product already peaks at height $6$.
Das unskalierte Produkt $-(x+1)(x-3)$ ist bei $x=1$ bereits $6$, daher ist die zum genannten Scheitel nötige Streckung $k=-1$.
Der Sensorweg ist $f(x)=-x+3$, weil eine Steigung $-1$ durch $(0,2)$ den Achsenabschnitt auf $3$ anhebt.
The sensor path und the clearance curve meet at exactly one real point.
At $x=1$ the sensor lies strictly below the clearance peak.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Falsch

Opening downwards mit those roots means $g(x)=k(x+1)(x-3)$ für some $k<0$. The unscaled choice $k=-1$ still has to hit height $6$ at the named peak $x=1$.

$$-(1+1)(1-3)=-(2)(-2)$$

$$h=-(1+1)(1-3)$$

$$h=4$$

$$4\neq 6$$

The unscaled factorisation misses the named vertex height. A stretch other than $-1$ is required.

The stretch $k$ is fixed by the named vertex: $k(1+1)(1-3)=6$ forces $k=-3/2$, not the unscaled $-1$.

$$k=-\frac{3}{2}$$

The unscaled product does not already peak at height $6$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**B.** → Falsch

Evaluate the unscaled product at the named peak abscissa $x=1$; that value is its vertex height, und it is the stretch that would have to equal $6$.

$$
-(x+1)(x-3)\big|_{x = 1} = -(2)(-2) = 4
$$

$$4\neq 6$$

The unscaled vertex height is $4$, not $6$, so the stretch needed to hit the named vertex is not $k=-1$. Matching $k\cdot(-4)=6$ would force $k=-3/2$.

The unscaled product is $4$ at $x=1$, not $6$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**C.** → Falsch

A line is uniquely determined by its slope und a point. Slope $-1$ through $(0,2)$ is point-slope mit intercept $2$, not $3$.

$$f(x)=-1\cdot(x-0)+2$$

$$f(x)=-x+2$$

The claimed intercept $3$ would have required the line to pass through $(0,3)$ instead of the given $(0,2)$.

$$f(x)=-x+2\neq -x+3$$

Point-slope through $(0,2)$ never lifts the intercept. The claimed $+3$ would sein the intercept of a parallel line through $(0,3)$.

The intercept is $2$, not $3$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**D.** → Falsch

Scale so that $g(1)=6$: $k(2)(-2)=6$ forces $k=-3/2$. Then form the difference mit the sensor $f(x)=-x+2$.

$$g(x)=-\frac{3}{2}(x+1)(x-3)$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=-\frac{3}{2}x^{2}+4x+\frac{5}{2}$$

$$\Delta=16+15$$

$$\Delta=31$$

$$31>0$$

A positive discriminant gives two distinct real meetings, not one. Tangency would have required $\Delta=0$.

A quadratic difference mit positive discriminant cannot sein a perfect square, so tangency is out of reach für this pair.

The graphs meet twice, not once.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**E.** → Wahr

At the peak abscissa compare the sensor height mit the named vertex height $6$. Only the line is needed: the sensor is $f(x)=-x+2$.

$$f(1)=-1+2$$

$$f(1)=1$$

$$1<6$$

The sensor sits five units below the clearance peak. A meeting at $x=1$ would have required $f(1)=6$, which fails.

The clearance peak is the given point $(1,6)$, while the sensor at that abscissa is the much lower point $(1,1)$.

$$(1,1)\text{ sits below }(1,6)$$

The sensor lies strictly below the clearance peak.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
MATH 7.E10.solution_overview:
The clearance brief names a downward parabola by its vertex und its two deck meetings, together mit a sensor line through $(0,2)$ of slope $-1$. Those data determine both rules uniquely.

$$g(x)=a(x+1)(x-3)$$

The unscaled product $-(x+1)(x-3)$ already has the right roots und the right axis, but its height at $x=1$ is $4$, not $5$. The stretch $a$ must make up the missing unit.

$$-(1+1)(1-3)=4\neq 5$$

$$
a(2)(-2) = 5,\qquad a = -\frac{5}{4}
$$

The rebuilt clearance curve und the sensor path are therefore

$$
g(x) = -\frac{5}{4}(x+1)(x-3),\qquad f(x) = -x+2
$$

The claimed sensor $f(x)=-x+3$ would pass through $(0,3)$, not through the given point $(0,2)$. Meetings of $g$ mit the true sensor are the zeros of $g-f$; that discriminant is positive, so there are two real meetings rather than one.

$$
g(x)-f(x) = -\frac{5}{4}x^{2}+\frac{7}{2}x+\frac{7}{4},\qquad \Delta = 21
$$

At the crown abscissa $x=1$ the sensor sits at height $1$, strictly below the clearance peak $5$.

$$
g(1) = 5,\qquad f(1) = 1
$$

MATH 7.E11.title: Mulde berührt eine Niveaulinie
MATH 7.E11.context: A **solid brown parabola** $g$ und a **dashed green horizontal line** appear on the axes. Formulas are withheld. Decide each claim von the figure alone. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Der Extrempunkt der durchgezogenen Kurve liegt auf der gestrichelten Linie, und dieser gemeinsame Punkt ist der einzige Schnitt der beiden Spuren.

$$g(x)=(x-1)(x-3)$$

**B.** → Wahr

The two brown axis meetings sit at $x=1$ und $x=3$. Their midpoint is the marked trough at $x=2$, so each crossing is one unit von the turning abscissa.

$$g(x)=(x-1)(x-3)$$

$$x=1$$

$$x=3$$

$$\frac{1+3}{2}=2$$

The axis of a parabola always bisects the two roots, und here that midpoint is already the marked turn.

One unit on each side is the distance

$$|3-2|=|1-2|$$

$$x=|3-2|$$

$$x=1$$

which is also half the gap between the two roots.

The crossings sit equally far von the turning abscissa, one unit on each side.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**C.** → Falsch

An upward-opening parabola climbs without bound away von its trough, so it rises above any fixed horizontal line. Rebuild $g(x)=(x-1)(x-3)$ und test the arms.

$$g(0)=3$$

$$3>-1$$

$$g(4)=3$$

$$3>-1$$

On the figure the arms already sit above the dashed level near the window edges. The dashed line therefore cannot lie entirely above the solid curve.

$$g(x)\to+\infty\text{ as }|x|\to\infty$$

The dashed line is not entirely above the solid curve.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**D.** → Falsch

The dashed level cuts the trough at its lowest point und nowhere else: that is a tangency, not a pair of crossings.

$$g(x)+1=(x-2)^{2}$$

$$(x-2)^{2}=0$$

$$x=2$$

A square has a repeated root, so there is exactly one shared point, und it is the Extrempunkt. Two meetings distinct von the vertex would have required a positive discriminant.

There is exactly one shared point, und it is the Extrempunkt.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**E.** → Wahr

The axis of a parabola always bisects the two roots, so the turning abscissa is the midpoint of the two axis crossings.

$$g(x)=(x-1)(x-3)$$

$$x=\frac{1+3}{2}$$

$$x=\frac{4}{2}$$

$$x=2$$

The figure agrees: the marked trough sits halfway between the two brown meetings mit the horizontal axis.

$$g(2)=-1$$

That midpoint identity is the axis formula $x=-b/(2a)$ in disguise: für $g(x)=x^{2}-4x+3$ one has $4/2=2$.

$$x=-\frac{-4}{2}$$

$$x=2$$

The midpoint of the crossings is the turning abscissa.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
MATH 7.E11.solution_overview:
The figure withholds formulas, so recover the solid parabola von the marked trough und the two axis crossings, und recover the dashed level von its constant height.

$$
g(x) = x^{2}-4x+3,\qquad y = -1
$$

The brown curve öffnet sich nach oben (a trough, not a peak) und meets the horizontal axis at $x=1$ und $x=3$. Completing the square places the vertex exactly on the dashed line.

$$
g(x) = (x-2)^{2}-1,\qquad \mathrm{ver} = \left(2,-1\right)
$$

Because the vertex height equals the dashed level, the line is tangent to the parabola at the trough: they share exactly one point, not two, und the line does not sit entirely above the curve.

$$
g(x)+1 = (x-2)^{2},\qquad \Delta = 0
$$

Coefficients of $g$ confirm the same geometry: positive Leitkoeffizient, two real roots, axis $x=2$.

$$
a = 1>0,\qquad S = 4,\qquad P = 3,\qquad \Delta_{g} = 4
$$

$$
x = 1,\qquad x = 3
$$

MATH 7.E12.title: Arithmetische Stichproben — warum ein Quadrat nicht passt
MATH 7.E12.context: The table lists values of an unknown rule $y(x)$ at five equally spaced inputs. No formula is printed. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Die ersten Differenzen der $y$-Zeile sind konstant $3$, daher verschwinden die zweiten Differenzen und der Interpolationsgrad ist höchstens $1$.
The unique line through the first und last listed points has slope $2$.
Extending the constant-gap pattern one step past $x=4$ und one step before $x=0$ produces $y(5)=14$ und $y(-1)=-4$.
Die zweiten Differenzen der $y$-Zeile verschwinden alle, daher ist jedes Interpolationspolynom vom Grad höchstens zwei tatsächlich eine Gerade.
A quadratic mit Leitkoeffizient $1$ cannot fit every listed point.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Form neighbouring gaps of the $y$-row. The five listed heights are $-1,2,5,8,11$.

$$
2-(-1)=3,\qquad 5-2 = 3,\qquad 8-5 = 3,\qquad 11-8 = 3
$$
