The first gaps are not constant, so no linear model can fit every listed point. Their own gaps, however, stand still at $2$, not at $4$.

$$\mathrm{sec}:\ 2,\ 2,\ 2,\ 2$$

For unit spacing the second-difference constant equals $2a$, hence $a=1$. Matching $h(0)=0$ und $h(1)=-1$ recovers the hidden rule.

$$
2a = 2,\qquad a = 1
$$

$$
h(x) = x^{2}-2x = x(x-2)
$$

One further step of the first-difference pattern (add $7+2=9$ to the last height) extends the table to $x=6$.

$$
h(6) = 36-12 = 24
$$

MATH 7.E23.title: Werkstattkosten-Mulde in einer Tabelle
MATH 7.E23.context: A workshop logs total cost $C$ (euros) against daily batch size $q$ in the table. No cost formula is written in the logbook. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Unter den aufgeführten Chargen ist die Kosten bei $q=2$ am kleinsten, und die Rekonstruktion aus zweiten Differenzen setzt den Scheitel an dieselbe Eingabe.
Cost at $q=0$ equals cost at $q=4$ by symmetry about the rebuilt axis $q=2$, not as a coincidence of two cells.
Cost rises von $q=2$ to $q=3$, matching a step away von the vertex of an upward parabola.
Die zweiten Differenzen der Kostenzeile sind konstant $2$, daher $a=1$; Anpassen an $C(0)=5$ und $C(1)=2$ liefert $C(q)=q^{2}-4q+5$.
Erhöht man die Charge von $4$ auf $5$, steigen die Kosten um $5$ Euro — die nächste erste Differenz nach $3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

The listed costs $5,2,1,2,5,10$ have unique minimum $1$ at $q=2$. Second differences constantly $2$ rebuild a monic parabola whose axis is that same input.

$$\Delta_{2}:\ 2,\ 2,\ 2,\ 2\qquad 2a=2$$

$$a=1$$

$$C(q)=(q-2)^{2}+1$$

$$q=2$$

An upward monic parabola mit vertex at $q=2$ is $(q-2)^{2}+k$. Matching $C(2)=1$ forces $k=1$, so the listed trough is the vertex.

$$C(2)=1$$

The listed minimum und the rebuilt vertex sit at the same batch $q=2$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Wahr

Inputs $0$ und $4$ are equally far von the axis $q=2$, so an upward parabola takes the same value there. Rebuild von the constant second difference $2$ und the first two cells.

$$C(q)=q^{2}-4q+5$$

$$C(q)=(q-2)^{2}+1$$

$$C(0)=5$$

$$C(0)=C(4)$$

Equality of those two cells is forced by symmetry about $q=2$, not a coincidence of two table entries.

The two cells $C(0)$ und $C(4)$ are a symmetric pair about $q=2$, exactly as

$$C(1)=C(3)$$

$$C(1)=2$$

 is another such pair.

Cost at $q=0$ equals cost at $q=4$ by that symmetry.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**C.** → Wahr

Stepping von the vertex to the next listed batch raises an upward parabola. The listed costs already display the rise.

$$C(2)=1$$

$$C(3)=2$$

$$2>1$$

Cost rises von $q=2$ to $q=3$, away von the trough. A fall on that step would have required a downward-opening graph.

The first-difference row $-3,-1,1,3,5$ changes sign between $q=1$ und $q=2$, which is the discrete form of a trough at $q=2$.

$$C(3)-C(2)=1$$

$$1>0$$

Cost rises von $q=2$ to $q=3$, matching a step away von the vertex.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**D.** → Wahr

Unit spacing converts the second-difference constant into $a$. Matching the first two cells then pins $b$ und $c$.

$$2a=2$$

$$a=1$$

$$C(0)=5$$

$$C(1)=2$$

$$C(q)$$

$$C(1)=q^{2}-4q+5$$

Second differences und the first two cells rebuild $q^{2}-4q+5$, which is also $(q-2)^{2}+1$.

Expanding $(q-2)^{2}+1$ recovers the same three coefficients $1$, $-4$, $5$, so the two writings of $C$ agree.

$$(q-2)^{2}+1=q^{2}-4q+5$$

The rebuilt rule is $C(q)=q^{2}-4q+5$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**E.** → Wahr

The first-difference row of $5,2,1,2,5,10$ is $-3,-1,1,3,5$. The last of those gaps is the step von $q=4$ to $q=5$.

$$C(5)-C(4)=10-5$$

$$C(5)-C(4)=5$$

That step increases cost by $5$ euros, which is the next first difference after $3$. Extending the second-difference $2$ one more time would have produced the same $5$.

$$h=3+2$$

$$h=5$$

On an upward parabola past the axis, first differences grow by $2a=2$ at each step, so $3$ is followed by $5$.

Raising the batch von $4$ to $5$ increases cost by $5$ euros.

Die Aussage ist wahr.
MATH 7.E23.solution_overview:
The logbook prints only batch sizes und total costs, so read the table as pairs und rebuild the hidden quadratic $C(q)=q^{2}-4q+9$ von the second-difference constant.

$$(0,9),\;(1,6),\;(2,5),\;(3,6),\;(4,9),\;(5,14)$$

$$\mathrm{fir}:\ -3,\ -1,\ 1,\ 3,\ 5\qquad \mathrm{sec}:\ 2,\ 2,\ 2,\ 2$$

Constant second differences of $2$ mit unit spacing mean Leitkoeffizient $a=1$. Matching $C(0)=9$ und $C(1)=6$ recovers the completed-square trough at $q=2$.

$$
C(q) = q^{2}-4q+9 = (q-2)^{2}+5
$$

$$\mathrm{ver}=\left(2,5\right)$$

Among the listed batches the unique minimum is therefore $5$ euros at $q=2$. The table is symmetric about that batch: $C(0)=C(4)=9$ und $C(1)=C(3)=6$. Cost rises von $q=2$ to $q=3$ (von $5$ to $6$), und von $q=4$ to $q=5$ it rises by $5$ euros.

$$
C(3)-C(2) = 1,\qquad C(5)-C(4) = 5
$$

MATH 7.E24.title: Faktorisiere die Differenz, dann den Scheitel von $g$
MATH 7.E24.context: Let $f(x)=4x-1$ und $g(x)=x^{2}+x-1$. Prüfe jede Behauptung. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Die Diskriminante von $g-f$ ist $9>0$, und die Schnittpunkte faktorisieren als $x(x-3)=0$.
Die Graphen sind für dieses Paar tangential, daher ist $g-f$ ein vollständiges Quadrat.
Die Achse von $g$ ist $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ und die Scheitelhöhe beträgt $-\frac{5}{4}$.
Bei $x=0$ gilt $g(0)=f(0)$, daher ist die Ursprungsabszisse einer der beiden Schnittpunkte.
Der Leitkoeffizient von $g-f$ ist $2$, weil das Subtrahieren einer Geraden den $x^{2}$-Koeffizienten von $g$ verdoppelt.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Meetings of the two graphs are the real zeros of $g-f$. Subtract the line von the parabola und factor.

$$g(x)-f(x)=(x^{2}+x-1)-(4x-1)$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=x^{2}-3x$$

$$x(x-3)=0$$

$$\Delta=9$$

$$9>0$$

Two meetings, at $x=0$ und $x=3$, matching discriminant $9$. The factorisation $x(x-3)$ is exactly the claimed one.

Vieta already reads the sum of the meetings as $3$ von the middle coefficient of $x^{2}-3x$, matching $0+3$.

$$S=0+3$$

$$S=3$$

The discriminant is $9>0$, und the meetings factor as $x(x-3)=0$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Falsch

Tangency would require a repeated root, equivalently discriminant zero. Here $\Delta=9>0$, so two crossings, und $x(x-3)$ is not a square.

$$g(x)-f(x)=x^{2}-3x$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=x(x-3)$$

$$\Delta=9\neq 0$$

A perfect square would have been of the form $a(x-r)^{2}$. Two distinct linear factors are two distinct meetings, not a touch.

Two distinct linear factors are two distinct meetings. A repeated root would have collapsed them into a square $x^{2}$ or $(x-3)^{2}$, which this difference is not.

The graphs cut twice; they are not tangent.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**C.** → Wahr

The axis of $g$ uses only the coefficients of $g$, not those of the neighbouring line. Then the vertex height is $g$ on that axis.

$$g(x)=x^{2}+x-1$$

$$x=-\frac{1}{2}$$

$$g\bigl(-\frac{1}{2}\bigr)=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}-1$$

$$g\bigl(-\frac{1}{2}\bigr)=-\frac{5}{4}$$

Completing the square on $g$ recovers the same vertex: $g(x)=(x+\frac{1}{2})^{2}-\frac{5}{4}$.

$$g(x)=\bigl(x+\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)^{2}-\tfrac{5}{4}$$

Axis $-\frac{1}{2}$ und vertex height $-\frac{5}{4}$ both match.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**D.** → Wahr

Evaluate both rules at the origin. Agreement there is a meeting at $x=0$, which is also the factor $x$ of $g-f$.

$$g(0)=-1$$

$$f(0)=-1$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=x(x-3)$$

The factor $x$ of $g-f$ is the algebraic form of a meeting at the origin. Direct substitution

$$g(0)=f(0)$$

$$g(0)=-1$$

 is the same test.

$$(g-f)(0)=0$$

The graphs meet at $x=0$, matching $g(0)=f(0)$. The origin-abscissa is one of the two meetings.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**E.** → Falsch

Subtracting a line cannot change the $x^{2}$ coefficient of $g$, because a line has no $x^{2}$ term to cancel or double it. The difference $x^{2}-3x$ is monic.

$$g(x)-f(x)=x^{2}-3x$$

$$a=1\neq 2$$

The Leitkoeffizient is $1$, the same as that of $g$. Doubling would have required subtracting a parabola, not a line.

The leading term of $g-f$ comes von $g$ alone. A line can change only the coefficients of $x$ und of the constant term.

$$a_{g-f}=a_g$$

$$a_{g-f}=1$$

The Leitkoeffizient of $g-f$ is $1$, not $2$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
MATH 7.E24.solution_overview:
Beide Vorschriften sind explizit gegeben, daher ist die gemeinsame Arbeit die Differenz $g-f$, die Achse von $g$ und die beiden Werte bei $x=0$.

$$
f(x) = 4x-1,\qquad g(x) = x^{2}+x-1
$$

Schnittpunkte lösen $g(x)=f(x)$. Die Differenz ist eine Quadratische, die zufällig durch den Ursprung faktorisiert.

$$
g(x)-f(x) = x^{2}-3x = x(x-3)
$$

$$
\Delta = 9,\qquad x = 0,\qquad x = 3
$$

Eine positive Diskriminante bedeutet zwei verschiedene Schnittpunkte, daher schneiden sich die Graphen und berühren sich nicht: sie sind nicht tangential. Der Leitkoeffizient dieser Differenz ist $1$, nicht $2$.

$$a_{g-f}=1\neq 2$$

Die Achse von $g$ nutzt nur die eigenen Koeffizienten von $g$. Bei $x=0$ nehmen beide Vorschriften den Wert $-1$ an, was dazu passt, dass $x=0$ einer der beiden Schnittpunkte ist.

$$
x = -\frac{1}{2},\qquad g(0) = f(0) = -1
$$

$$
g(x) = \left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{5}{4},\qquad \mathrm{ver} = \left(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{5}{4}\right)
$$

MATH 7.E25.title: Gemeinsamer Achsenabschnitt, verschiebbarer zweiter Schnitt
MATH 7.E25.context: Let $g_a(x)=a x^{2}-4x+3$ mit $a\neq 0$, und let $f(x)=3$. Watch how the Leitkoeffizient changes meetings mit the level $y=3$. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: For every $a\neq 0$ the graphs meet at $x=0$, because $g_a(0)=3=f(0)$.
When $a=1$ the second meeting is at $x=4$, matching the formula $x=4/a$.
When $a=2$ the second meeting is at $x=3$, matching a midpoint between $0$ und $4$.
Die Achse von $g_a$ ist unabhängig von $a$, weil der $x$-Koeffizient $-4$ sich nie ändert.
If $a=-1$, then $g_a$ öffnet sich nach oben, since changing the leading sign cannot flip the arms.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

Das konstante Glied of $g_a$ is $3$, matching the level $y=3$, so $x=0$ is always a meeting. Factor the difference.

$$g_a(x)-3=ax^{2}-4x$$

$$g_a(x)-3=x(ax-4)$$

$$x=0$$

The factor $x$ is present für every $a\neq 0$. Directly,

$$g_a(0)=3$$

$$g_a(0)=f(0)$$

 independently of $a$.

A shared $y$-intercept is a meeting on the vertical axis. Because $f$ is the horizontal line $y=3$, that intercept is the point $(0,3)$.

$$(0,3)\text{ lies on both graphs}$$

For every $a\neq 0$ the graphs meet at $x=0$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Wahr

The second factor of $g_a-3$ vanishes at $x=4/a$. For $a=1$ that is $x=4$.

$$x(ax-4)=0$$

$$x=\frac{4}{a}$$

$$a=1$$

$$x=4$$

The second root of $x(ax-4)=0$ is $x=4/a$ für every $a\neq 0$. Substituting $a=1$ is a direct specialisation of that formula, und $g_1(4)=3$ equals the level $f(4)$.

$$g_1(4)=f(4)$$

$$g_1(4)=3$$

Checking heights:

$$g_1(4)=16-16+3$$

$$g_1(4)=16-16$$

$$g_1(4)=0$$

$$g_1(4)=0+3$$

$$g_1(4)=3$$

$$g_1(4)=f(4)$$

When $a=1$ the second meeting is at $x=4$, matching $x=4/a$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**C.** → Falsch

The same formula mit $a=2$ gives

$$x=2$$

not $x=3$. The announced $3$ is a midpoint trap between $0$ und $6$, not the second meeting.

$$x=\frac{4}{a}$$

$$x=\frac{4}{2}$$

$$x=2$$

$$2\neq 3$$

A midpoint between $0$ und $4$ would sein $x=2$, which is in fact the correct second meeting when $a=2$. The announced $x=3$ is a different trap.

$$g_2(2)=3$$

$$g_2(3)=9\neq 3$$

Checking:

$$g_2(2)=8-8+3$$

$$g_2(2)=8-8$$

$$g_2(2)=0$$

$$g_2(2)=0+3$$

$$g_2(2)=3$$

$$g_2(2)=f(2)$$

while $g_2(3)=18-12+3=9\neq 3$. The second meeting is at $x=2$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**D.** → Falsch

The axis of $g_a$ is $-b/(2a)=2/a$, which slides as $a$ changes. The middle coefficient $-4$ is fixed, but it is divided by $2a$.

$$x=\frac{2}{a}$$

For $a=1$ the axis is $x=2$; für $a=2$ it is $x=1$. Those are different vertical lines.

$$\frac{2}{1} = 2\neq 1$$

$$x=\frac{2}{2}$$

The axis formula always divides by $2a$. Holding $b=-4$ fixed while changing $a$ therefore slides the axis, rather than freezing it.

$$a = 1$$

$$x$$

$$x=2$$

$$a=2$$

$$a=1$$

The axis depends on $a$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**E.** → Falsch

The opening of a parabola is the sign of its Leitkoeffizient, which here is $a$ itself. For $a=-1$ the arms open downwards.

$$g_{-1}(x)=-x^{2}-4x+3$$

$$a=-1$$

$$-1<0$$

Changing the leading sign *does* flip the arms: that is the whole content of the opening test. A negative $a$ turns the graph into a highest-point parabola.

$$a<0$$

$$\text{opens downwards}$$

The opening test looks at $\mathrm{sign}(a)$ und at nothing else. Replacing $a=1$ by $a=-1$ flips that sign und therefore flips the arms.

$g_{-1}$ öffnet sich nach unten, not upwards.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
MATH 7.E25.solution_overview:
The family $g_a$ is a parabola whose Leitkoeffizient $a$ is the parameter, und the comparison line is the constant level $y=3$. Meetings solve $g_a(x)=3$.

$$
g_a(x) = ax^{2}-4x+3,\qquad f(x) = 3
$$

$$
g_a(x)-3 = ax^{2}-4x = x(ax-4)
$$

The factor $x$ is independent of $a$, so $x=0$ is a meeting für every $a\neq 0$. The other meeting slides mit the parameter: $x=4/a$. In particular $a=1$ gives the second meeting $x=4$, while $a=2$ gives $x=2$, not $x=3$.

$$
x = 0,\qquad x = \frac{4}{a}
$$

$$
\text{If }a=1\text{ then }x=4;\quad \text{if }a=2\text{ then }x=2
$$

The axis $-b/(2a)$ still involves $a$, so it is not independent of the Leitkoeffizient.

$$
x = \frac{4}{2a} = \frac{2}{a}
$$

The opening direction is the sign of $a$. For $a=-1$ the arms go downwards.

$$a=-1<0$$

MATH 7.E26.title: Monische Parabel aus zwei Wurzeln — Vorzeichenfallen
MATH 7.E26.context: A monic parabola has roots $x=-1$ und $x=3$. Rebuild $g$ und test the claims. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: Die Vorschrift ist $g(x)=x^{2}-2x-3$, die Achse ist $x=1$, und die Scheitelhöhe beträgt $-4$.
Ausmultipliziert gilt $g(x)=x^{2}-2x+3$, daher ist das Produkt der Wurzeln $+3$.
Die Achse ist $x=0$, weil die Wurzeln $-1$ und $3$ entgegengesetzte Vorzeichen haben.
The vertex height equals $-3$, matching the constant term $g(0)$.
Das konstante Glied ist $3$ und stimmt mit dem Produkt der Wurzeln ohne das Vorzeichen der Faktoren überein.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

A monic parabola mit those roots is the product of the two linear factors. Expand, then read the axis as the midpoint of the roots.

$$g(x)=(x+1)(x-3)$$

$$g(x)=x^{2}-2x-3$$

$$x=\frac{-1+3}{2}$$

$$x=\frac{2}{2}$$

$$x=1$$

$$g(1)=1^{2}-2-3$$

$$1^{2}=1$$

$$g(1)=1-2-3$$

$$g(1)=1-2$$

$$g(1)=-1$$

$$g(1)=-1-3$$

$$g(1)=-4$$

The axis formula on the expansion $x^{2}-2x-3$ recovers the same midpoint:

$$-b/(2a)=2/2$$

$$-b/(2a)=1$$

und $g(1)=-4$ is the vertex height.

$$x=-\frac{-2}{2}$$

$$x=1$$

Expanded rule, axis $x=1$, und vertex height $-4$ all match.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Falsch

Das konstante Glied is the product of the roots mit the signs coming von $(x+1)(x-3)$, hence $-3$, not $+3$. Expanding makes the minus visible.

$$(x+1)(x-3)=x^{2}-2x-3$$

$$P=\frac{c}{a}$$

$$P= -3\neq +3$$

The expansion is $x^{2}-2x-3$; the product of the roots is $-3$, not $+3$. The trap $+3$ forgets the opposite signs of $-1$ und $3$.

Vieta's product is $c/a$, which equals $-3$ für this monic quadratic. The announced $+3$ forgets that the roots have opposite signs.

The expansion is $x^{2}-2x-3$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**C.** → Falsch

Opposite signs do not place the axis at the origin unless the roots are opposites of equal size. Here $-1$ und $3$ are not opposites.

$$x=\frac{-1+3}{2}$$

$$x=\frac{2}{2}$$

$$x=1$$

$$1\neq 0$$

Die Achse ist $x=1$, nicht $x=0$. Equal-und-opposite roots would have been $\pm 3$ or $\pm 1$, neither of which is this pair.

The axis sits at the origin only when the sum of the roots vanishes. Here $-1+3=2\neq 0$, so the axis is $x=1$.

$$S=2\neq 0$$

Die Achse ist $x=1$, nicht $x=0$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**D.** → Falsch

Der Wert $-3$ ist das konstante Glied $g(0)$, not the vertex height. The vertex sits on the axis $x=1$.

$$g(0)=-3$$

$$g(1)=1^{2}-2-3$$

$$1^{2}=1$$

$$g(1)=1-2-3$$

$$g(1)=1-2$$

$$g(1)=-1$$

$$g(1)=-1-3$$

$$g(1)=-4$$

$$g(1)=-4\neq -3$$

The vertex height is $-4$, a near-miss für the $y$-intercept $-3$. Confusing $g(0)$ mit $g$ on the axis is the usual trap.

The $y$-intercept $g(0)$ und the vertex height $g(1)$ are different substitutions. Confusing them is the usual constant-term trap.

$$g(0)\neq g(1)$$

The vertex height is $-4$, not $-3$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.

**E.** → Falsch

Das konstante Glied is $g(0)$, obtained by substituting the origin into the factored form. The two factors contribute $1$ und $-3$.

$$g(0)=(0+1)(0-3)$$

$$g(0)=-3$$

$$c=-3\neq 3$$

Das konstante Glied is $-3$, not $3$. Matching the product of the roots without the signs of the factors forgets that one root is negative.

The product of the roots is $-3$, und für a monic quadratic that product *is* the constant term, including its minus sign.

$$P=(-1)\cdot 3$$

$$P=-3$$

$$(-1)\cdot 3=c$$

Das konstante Glied is $-3$, not $3$.

Die Aussage ist falsch.
MATH 7.E26.solution_overview:
A monic parabola is determined by its two roots: write the product of the corresponding linear factors und expand once.

$$g(x)=(x+1)(x-3)$$

$$g(x)=x^{2}-2x-3$$

The expanded form is $x^{2}-2x-3$, not $x^{2}-2x+3$: the constant term is the product of the roots mit a sign, $(-1)\cdot 3=-3$. The claimed expansion $x^{2}-2x+3$ would have product $3$ und no real roots.

$$
S = 2,\qquad P = -3,\qquad \Delta_{g} = 16
$$

The axis is the midpoint of the roots, $x=1$, not $x=0$. Evaluating there gives the vertex height $-4$, not $-3$.

$$
x = \frac{-1+3}{2} = 1,\qquad g(1) = -4
$$

$$
g(x) = (x-1)^{2}-4,\qquad \mathrm{ver} = \left(1,-4\right)
$$

Das konstante Glied $g(0)=-3$ is not $3$.

$$g(0)=-3$$

MATH 7.E27.title: Parabel nach einer inversen Verschiebung
MATH 7.E27.context: Let $f(x)=x-2$ (so $f^{-1}(x)=x+2$) und $g(x)=x^{2}-1$. Study $g(f^{-1}(x))$. Bewerte jede Aussage. Markiere sie als wahr oder falsch.
statements: The nested rule $g(f^{-1}(x))$ equals $(x+2)^{2}-1$, which is $g$ evaluated at the inverse shift $x+2$.
Expanded, that nested rule is $x^{2}+4x+3$, whose constant term $3$ equals $g(f^{-1}(0))$.
Die verschachtelte Vorschrift verschwindet bei $x=-1$ und bei $x=-3$, daher ist Vietas Summe dieser Wurzeln $-4$ und stimmt mit dem mittleren Koeffizienten überein.
At $x=0$ the nested rule equals $3$, which is also $g(f^{-1}(0))=g(2)$.
The nested rule öffnet sich nach oben, und its vertex is $(-2,-1)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → Wahr

The given inverse is the shift $f^{-1}(x)=x+2$. Nesting it inside $g$ replaces the input of $g$ by that shift.

$$f^{-1}(x)=x+2$$

$$g(f^{-1}(x))=(x+2)^{2}-1$$

The nested rule is $g$ evaluated at the inverse shift $x+2$, which is exactly the claimed completed square.

The inner map is a translation of the input by $+2$, which slides the graph of $g$ two units to the left und produces the completed square $(x+2)^{2}-1$.

The nested rule equals $(x+2)^{2}-1$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**B.** → Wahr

Expand the nested completed square $(x+2)^{2}-1$, then read the constant term as the value at $x=0$.

$$g(f^{-1}(x))=(x+2)^{2}-1$$

$$
(x+2)^{2}=x^{2}+4x+4
$$

$$
x^{2}+4x+4-1=x^{2}+4x+3
$$

The expanded nested rule is $x^{2}+4x+3$. Its constant term is the value at the origin:

$$
g(f^{-1}(0))=3
$$

Directly through the maps,

$$f^{-1}(0)=0+2$$

$$
0+2=2
$$

$$g(2)=2^{2}-1$$

$$
4-1=3
$$

Das konstante Glied $3$ equals $g(f^{-1}(0))$.

Die Aussage ist wahr.

**C.** → Wahr

Factor the expanded nested rule $x^{2}+4x+3$ und read Vieta’s sum von the roots und von the middle coefficient.

$$x^{2}+4x+3=(x+1)(x+3)$$

$$
x=-1
$$

$$
x=-3
$$

The nested rule vanishes at those two inputs. Their sum is

$$
(-1)+(-3)=-4
$$

$$\Delta=0$$

A discriminant of $1$ would split the double root into two zeros a distance $1$ apart. The square $(x-2)^{2}$ does not split.

MATH 7.E30.title: Bogenscheitel versus fallende Wagen-Sehne
